title: Molecular geometry (VSEPR) and polarity
note: VSEPR: electron regions around a central atom (bonds of any order, or lone pairs) spread as far apart as possible. The electron-pair geometry counts all regions; the molecular shape names only where atoms are. Lone pairs take more room and squeeze bond angles. A molecule is polar if it has polar bonds whose dipoles do not cancel.

read.title: Shape decides polarity
text: Valence shell electron-pair repulsion (VSEPR) theory predicts shape from a simple count. Around a central atom, every bond and every lone pair is one region of electron density, whether the bond is single, double, or triple. These regions repel each other and spread as far apart as they can. Two regions give a straight line at 180°, three give a flat triangle at 120°, four give a tetrahedron at 109.5°, five give a trigonal bipyramid, and six give an octahedron.

The shape we name, though, describes only the atoms. Ammonia has four regions, three bonds and one lone pair, so its electron-pair geometry is tetrahedral, but its molecular shape is a trigonal pyramid. Water has two bonds and two lone pairs, so it is bent. Lone pairs spread out more than bonding pairs, pushing the bonds closer together: water's angle is about 104.5°, not 109.5°.

Shape matters because it decides polarity. Each polar bond has a dipole, an arrow of charge separation. In linear CO₂ the two C=O dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel, so the molecule is nonpolar. In bent water the O–H dipoles do not cancel, so water is polar. That polarity is why water dissolves salts and has such a high boiling point for its size.
